content: Schizophrenia is a severe psychiatric disorder characterized by significant disruptions in thought processes, which can affect language, perception, and self-awareness. Patients often experience psychotic symptoms, such as auditory hallucinations or delusions. Globally, over 21 million individuals are affected by schizophrenia, accounting for approximately 1.1% of worldwide disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). In China, while comprehensive epidemiological data on schizophrenia is lacking, a 1994 study in a specific region reported lifetime prevalence rates ranging from 0.426% in rural areas to 0.711% in urban areas among individuals aged 15 years and older. The onset of schizophrenia typically occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood and is influenced by a combination of genetic predisposition, perinatal and early childhood stress, and environmental factors. The diagnosis of schizophrenia is made through a detailed clinical interview conducted by a trained clinician, adhering to established diagnostic criteria such as the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) or the ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition). These criteria rely on self-reported symptoms and observed behavioral abnormalities, followed by a clinical evaluation to rule out other medical or psychiatric conditions. Schizophrenia is considered a treatable condition, with current management strategies primarily involving antipsychotic medications, psychological therapies, social support, and rehabilitation programs. Additionally, alternative approaches, such as Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), have been employed. TCM, rooted in Chinese philosophy and culture, has been used for centuries to address various mental health conditions and is reputed to have fewer adverse effects compared to Western antipsychotics. Although TCM does not have a direct equivalent to schizophrenia as defined in Western medicine, ancient Chinese practitioners used herbal remedies to treat disorders resembling schizophrenia. One such herb, Ginkgo biloba, is now being used in modern clinical settings for schizophrenia. Ginkgo biloba, known as 银杏 (yínxìng) in Chinese, is an ancient tree species and the sole surviving member of the Ginkgophyta division. Native to China, it is now cultivated worldwide. The leaves and fruits of Ginkgo biloba have been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries, either as standalone herbal teas or in combination with other herbs. Modern medicine has developed standardized extracts of Ginkgo biloba, such as EGb 761, which was introduced in the 1990s by Dr. Willmar Schwabe Pharmaceuticals. EGb 761 is a well-characterized extract containing approximately 24% flavone glycosides (including quercetin, kaempferol, and isorhamnetin) and 6% terpene lactones (such as ginkgolides A, B, and C, and bilobalide). Other components include proanthocyanidins, glucose, rhamnose, organic acids, and ginkgolic acids. EGb 761 has been used to treat a variety of conditions, including hypertension, coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, asthma, and as an adjunct therapy for cancer. In psychiatric medicine, EGb 761 is often used as an adjunct to antipsychotic medications for the treatment of schizophrenia. It is believed to enhance the therapeutic effects of antipsychotics while mitigating their side effects. Most studies on the use of EGb 761 for schizophrenia have been conducted in China, although research has also been carried out in other countries, such as the United States and Turkey. The pharmacological effects of EGb 761 are attributed to its flavonoid and terpene lactone content, which exhibit antioxidant properties, free radical scavenging, anti-platelet aggregation, anti-thrombotic actions, and inhibition of apoptosis. Additionally, EGb 761 has been shown to accelerate nerve impulse transmission and facilitate synaptic communication. Ginkgo biloba is thought to play a role in the prevention and treatment of neurological disorders, including dementia, memory loss, stress, and anxiety. Its mechanisms of action may involve increasing cerebral blood flow, improving energy metabolism, and reducing oxidative stress. Dysfunction in dopaminergic neurotransmission is a key factor in the development of schizophrenia-like symptoms. EGb 761 has demonstrated beneficial effects on dopaminergic function in various brain regions, including the prefrontal cortex, striatum, limbic system, nucleus accumbens, paraventricular nucleus, mesolimbic system, and nigrostriatal pathway. These effects may underlie its therapeutic potential in schizophrenia. Ginkgo biloba is considered a classical TCM herb for disorders resembling schizophrenia. The standardized extract EGb 761 is widely used in modern clinical practice. Numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews have investigated the efficacy of EGb 761 in schizophrenia. For example, Singh (2010) reviewed six RCTs, Brondino (2013) included three RCTs, Chen (2015) analyzed eight RCTs, and Zheng (2016) examined three RCTs involving schizophrenia patients with tardive dyskinesia. Given the growing body of evidence, it is essential to maintain and update systematic reviews in this area to incorporate emerging research findings.
